questions.learningObjective: Find the stopping time under a steady deceleration
questions.stem: A cartographer's note asks how long a survey vehicle takes to stop from 20 metres per second under a steady deceleration of 5 metres per second squared.
questions.explanation: The speed falls by 5 m/s each second, so 20 m/s takes 20/5 = 4 s to reach zero. Deceleration is a rate of change of speed, and distance over speed would not give the time.

options.text: About 2 seconds, because the line falls 9.8 metres in the first second and 9.8 in the second.
options.misconception: treats the second second as equal to the first in a fall

questions.explanation: For a fall from rest, h = half g t squared, so t = the square root of 2h/g = the square root of 40/9.8 = 2.02 s. The speed builds during the fall, so a plain division is too small.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the correct calculation for a stopping time
questions.stem: A cartographer's note asks which calculation gives the stopping time for a cart slowing at a steady rate.

options.text: The stopping distance divided by the initial speed, since both are lengths over time.
options.misconception: divides a distance by a speed for a time

options.text: The initial speed divided by the stopping distance, since the deceleration scales with them.
options.misconception: inverts the ratio needed for a time

options.text: The square of the initial speed over twice the deceleration, which is the distance covered.
options.misconception: confuses the stopping distance with the stopping time

options.text: The initial speed divided by the deceleration, since that is the rate at which the speed falls.

questions.explanation: The stopping time is the initial speed over the deceleration, because the speed falls at that rate until it reaches zero. The square of the speed over twice the deceleration gives a distance.
questions.hint: Time equals speed over the rate of change.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: Read a velocity from a straight line on a velocity-time graph
questions.stem: A cartographer's note shows a velocity-time graph rising linearly from 4 m/s at t = 1 s to 10 m/s at t = 6 s, and asks for the velocity at t = 4 s.
questions.explanation: The rise covers 6 m/s over 5 s, and t = 4 s is 3 s past the start, so v = 4 + 6 x 3/5 = 7.6 m/s. Reading down from the peak would use the wrong end of the line.
questions.hint: Move along the straight line from the known point.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Displacement as the area under a graph
questions.learningObjective: Justify that the area under a velocity-time graph is a distance
questions.stem: A cartographer's note asks why the area under a velocity-time graph gives distance rather than speed.

options.text: Because the area has units of metres per second times seconds, which simplify to metres.
Because the area is always larger than the height of the graph, and a larger value means a distance.
options.misconception: relates area to distance by size rather than by units

options.text: Because the speed is the slope of the graph, and the area cannot be the same thing.
options.misconception: justifies the answer by contrast without units

options.text: Because the graph is measured in metres, and every area on such a graph is a distance.
options.misconception: reasons from the axis labels rather than the units

questions.explanation: The height is metres per second and the width is seconds, so the area carries units of metres. That dimensional argument is the reason, not the size of the area or the axis labels.
questions.hint: Check the units of height times width.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: Check a position claimed for a vehicle with a speed and an acceleration
questions.stem: A cartographer's note gives a cart with an initial speed of 4 m/s, a constant acceleration of 2 m/s per second squared, and a starting position of 10 metres.

options.text: The position after 5 s is 30 m, from 10 + 4 x 5 with no acceleration term.
options.misconception: leaves out the acceleration term of the position law

options.text: The position after 5 s is 55 m, from 10 + 4 x 5 + half x 2 x 25.
The position after 5 s is 45 m, from 10 + 4 x 5 + 2 x 5 x 5, using the full acceleration.
options.misconception: forgets to halve the acceleration term

options.text: The position after 5 s is 65 m, from 10 + 4 x 5 + 2 x 25, doubling the acceleration term.
options.misconception: doubles the acceleration term instead of halving it

questions.explanation: The position is 10 + v t + half a t squared = 10 + 20 + 25 = 55 m. The acceleration term is halved and the time is squared, and the starting position has to be included.
questions.hint: Start plus v t plus half a t squared.
